question: Assume the JTB definition of Knowledge, which suggests that "Knowledge is a Justified True Belief". If our only available epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, what are the two problems JTB runs into? Ignore Gettier problems.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: On a JTB analysis knowledge is not a primitive, it is a complex
of belief + truth + justification. With only Knowledge and Belief as
primitive epistemic locutions the truth / justification square cannot be
kept straight.

Truth x Justification gives in the ordinary taxonomy four places

* JTB = Knowledge
* JT¬B? i.e. justified true belief = Knowledge by JTB
* J¬TB = justified false belief
* ¬JTB = unjustified true belief
* ¬J¬TB = unjustified false belief

Knowledge is taken to entail belief, so the only thing a JTB
analysis can mark off from mere belief is the JTB cell. Every
proposition that is not known therefore has to be filed under the
single label ‘belief’. That is

1. an inability to keep justified false belief distinct from an
unjustified false belief, and more generally to keep justified belief
distinct from unjustified belief.  A justified false belief is, on JTB,
epistemically good but not knowledge because it is not true.  With
only the two primitives Knowledge / Belief the justification component
has to be expressed in terms of Knowledge or in terms of Belief. If it
is expressed in terms of Belief you get a regress of beliefs for
justification: p is justified by belief q, q by belief r, … ad
infinitum, so justification never terminates in a distinct epistemic
state.  If it is expressed in terms of Knowledge you have circularity:
p is justified because it is known, but p is known only if it is
justified.  In ordinary language the loss appears as the collapse of
justified false belief into mere belief, i.e. the loss of an
epistemically creditworthy non-knowledge state.

2. an inability to keep unjustified true belief distinct from a
justified true belief.  An unjustified true belief is true but not
knowledge.  On the JTB taxonomy it is forced into the single ‘belief’
bin together with justified false belief and unjustified false belief.
Hence you lose the distinction between a true belief that is lucky and
a true belief that is creditable, and justification becomes idle once
truth is secured.  That is the familiar regress / circularity
formulation in the other direction: if justification is tried to be
made out of further beliefs you have the infinite regress of
justification; if you try to stop the regress with knowledge you have
justification = knowledge and JTB is circular.

In practice the two cells that JTB needs but that a two-state
ontology cannot accommodate are the creditworthy but non-knowledge
justified false belief and the lucky but non-knowledge unjustified true
belief.  That is the 2×2 truth/justification collapse that is normally
displayed as the regress of beliefs-for-justification versus the
circularity of knowledge-for-justification.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The JTB picture with only Knowledge and Belief as resources for justification runs straight into the classic regress/terminus dilemma.

If a belief p is justified, its justification must itself be a justified belief q, and q in turn must be justified by a justified belief r, and so on. With only Belief and Knowledge available as the kinds of epistemic attitudes that can do justifying work, you cannot appeal to a non-doxastic warrant, so the chain of beliefs that is supposed to justify p has to be built out of further beliefs. That gives you an infinite regress of ever further justifying beliefs with no stopping point.

The alternative to letting the regress run forever is to stop the chain at some point and say that certain beliefs are justified simply in virtue of being held, i.e., to posit a class of basic or foundational beliefs that are taken as epistemically given. On a strictly belief/knowledge-only inventory that stopping point is just dogmatism: you end up with beliefs that are treated as justified even though they themselves enjoy no independent justification within the system, an arbitrary foundation for the rest of the justificatory structure. Those two pressures — endless justification or an arbitrary, ungrounded foundation — are the structural problems JTB faces once you restrict the epistemic menu to Knowledge and Belief alone.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: With only knowledge and belief in the toolbox, justification for a belief can only be supplied by another belief or by an item you already count as knowledge. That immediately generates the familiar regress worry: any belief you offer as a reason for p has to itself be justified, which demands a further belief/reason, and so on ad infinitum, with no non-question-begging way to halt the chain. The only way to stop the chain in principle is to posit some beliefs that are taken to be justified without themselves being justified by any further knowledge or belief — an arbitrary foundational stop or epistemic dogmatism. In other words JTB is forced either into an endless demand for further reasons or into resting the whole edifice on an unjustified, stipulated base, and neither option gives a satisfying account of justification on a purely belief/knowledge ontology.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: With only Knowledge and Belief as live epistemic options, the justification clause in JTB forces a justificatory chain that can’t be closed. First you get the familiar infinite regress: to justify belief B you need a further belief B1 that B is justified, to justify B1 you need B2, and so on, because any justifier you can appeal to will itself be a belief that then needs justification. If you try to avoid the regress you are left with having to stop the chain at some point. But the only states you have are Knowledge, which by definition already requires justification, and Belief, which by itself is not knowledge. So the stopping point can only be an unjustified but taken-for-granted belief. That is the problem of an arbitrary or dogmatic foundation: you have to posit a baseline belief that is simply accepted without justification, which makes the account of knowledge rest on an epistemically unmotivated fiat rather than on genuine justification.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With only Knowledge and Belief as our epistemic resources, justification for a belief can only be supplied by something we already know or by something we merely believe. That generates two standard pressures.

First, the regress problem. If a belief p is justified only insofar as it is supported by a further belief q, and q itself needs justification, then justification can only be secured by a still further belief r, and so on. On a demanding reading where the justifier itself must be known, you never actually get off the ground without an infinite chain of justifiers.

Second, if the chain cannot be infinite, you have to stop it somewhere. Stopping it means positing some beliefs that are taken to be justified without themselves being justified by further knowledge or belief. Those would be epistemically arbitrary or dogmatic foundational beliefs. In effect you are forced to accept a base of beliefs whose justification is simply assumed, which is the classic problem of an unjustified stopping point / foundational dogmatism.

So the JTB picture with only knowledge and belief available is squeezed between an unending regress of justifiers and having to arbitrarily halt the regress with basic beliefs that are not themselves justified.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: If justification is itself an epistemic state then with only knowledge and belief to work with every justification for a belief P has to be either a piece of knowledge or a further belief about P. 

That immediately gives the classic regress of justification: a belief is justified only if the beliefs that justify it are themselves justified, and those justifiers need justifiers, etc. There is no third epistemic state to stop the chain, so in principle you are driven to an infinite hierarchy of ever higher-order justifications.

Because the regress cannot be run forever in practice, the only way to halt it is to posit some beliefs that are taken as basic or self-warranting and are simply left unjustified. With the inventory restricted to knowledge and belief that stopping point is just an arbitrary foundational dogmatism: basic beliefs are accepted as the terminus of justification even though they are not themselves known or justified in the JTB sense, so knowledge collapses into well-founded but ultimately groundless belief. The justificatory role is then played by belief all the way down, which blurs the intended distinction between justified true belief as knowledge and mere true belief.

16.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With only Knowledge and Belief in the inventory the justification condition for JTB becomes self-consuming. 

First, any justified belief P must be justified by some further belief or beliefs Q1...Qn that the subject holds. If those Qs are only beliefs, they too must be justified in order for them to count as justifiers for P under JTB. That pushes the demand for a justifier one step back again, and so on. On the assumption that no belief can count as a justifier unless it is itself justified, you get an infinite regress of justifiers for justifiers.

Second, the regress can only be stopped, if it is to be stopped within the Knowledge/Belief inventory, by terminating the chain in beliefs that are not themselves justified. That is, you end up having to treat some set of basic beliefs as justified simply by being believed, or as justified simply in virtue of being known. The first option is an arbitrary, dogmatic foundation, the second collapses justification into knowledge. In either case you are forced to accept a class of epistemic states that are held to be justified without any further epistemic support, i.e. an ungrounded, dogmatic base for the whole JTB structure. That is the classic foundational/arbitrariness problem that appears alongside the regress when no third epistemic status between knowledge and mere belief is available.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With JTB the justification condition has to be cashable in the epistemic resources you already have. If the only resources are Knowledge and Belief, then the reason you give for P must itself be a belief Q. Q is itself a belief, so on the JTB picture it too needs justification, and whatever justifies Q is a further belief R, and so on. That is the classic infinite regress of ever higher-order beliefs about beliefs.

The regress can only be stopped by allowing a chain to bottom out. But bottoming out on the resources here means either bottoming out in a belief that is treated as a terminus of justification even though it is not itself justified, i.e. a dogmatic or arbitrary stopping point, or bottoming out in a knowledge claim that already presupposes the very justification you are trying to secure. In either case you end up with an epistemic gap: you need a foundational class of beliefs that are taken to be justified in virtue of being held, or you need to posit a primitive knowledge base that is not itself produced by JTB, so the account can no longer explain how a mere belief is transformed into knowledge without smuggling in an extra epistemic status. That is why JTB on a two-state inventory faces the regress problem together with the problem of having to appeal to unjustified, essentially dogmatic foundations to block the regress.

4.text:
With JTB knowledge = justified true belief the epistemic taxonomy is exhausted by

* K = justified & true & believed
* B = not-K

so every non-knowledge state is just *belief*. Belief therefore has to do the work of four distinct intuitive states: justified true, unjustified true, justified false and unjustified false. The category B is then massively heterogeneous.

That gives you two independent collapses.

1. **Justified false belief is conflated with unjustified false belief.**  
A JFB is epistemically valuable in the way an unjustified false belief is not, but on JTB with only K and B it is not knowledge because it is false and it is not a distinct epistemic kind, it is just belief. Justification therefore ceases to matter for the class of false beliefs: justified false belief and unjustified false belief are both simply ‘belief’.

2. **Unjustified true belief is conflated with false belief.**  
An UTB is true in a way a false belief is not, but on JTB with only K and B it is not knowledge because it is unjustified and it is not a distinct epistemic kind, it is just belief. Truth therefore ceases to matter for the class of non-justified beliefs: an unjustified true belief and an unjustified false belief, and indeed a justified false belief, are all simply ‘belief’.

Hence Belief ends up lumping together justified with unjustified and true with false. JTB cannot capture the independent epistemic value of justification apart from truth and the independent epistemic value of truth apart from justification. That is the classic need for intermediate states such as justified belief, true belief, justified false belief, etc., which the two-state K / B taxonomy cannot accommodate.

3.text:
Under JTB

K p  iff  B p & T p & J p

and with only the two labels K and B to work with the four J x T cells
are forced into two bins

J T : JTB = Knowledge
J ~T : justified false belief
~J T : unjustified true belief
~J ~T : unjustified false belief

are all mapped onto B except the first one. That coarse graining is
the trouble.

* Justification does not entail truth. A subject can be fully justified
in holding p and still be wrong. JFB is on the same epistemic
label as an unjustified false belief, mere Belief. With only K and B
at our disposal we have no way to mark the epistemically responsible
false belief off from an irresponsible false belief, justification is
lost as soon as the belief turns out false.

* Truth does not entail justification. A subject can believe p truly
by luck, coincidence, wishful thinking etc., and p will still be
only a Belief. JTB therefore makes an unjustified true belief
epistemically indistinguishable from a justified false belief: both are
just Belief. In particular the epistemic value of justification for a
true belief is invisible until the belief is made true, and the
epistemic responsibility carried by a justified false belief is
invisible once the belief is false. That is the familiar justified-false
belief / accidental-true-belief gap which forces the whole J × T
space into the Knowledge / Belief dichotomy.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: On a JTB analysis Knowledge = True + Justified + Belief. If the ontology of doxastic states is really exhausted by Knowledge and Belief, then Belief is the residual class of everything that is not Knowledge.

That residual class is heterogeneous.

* Justified false belief. A belief can be justified and still false. By JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not true, so on a binary taxonomy it must be counted as Belief. Belief is then used to cover a justified state of error, and it is indistinguishable from an unjustified state of error. We lose the ability to mark warranted error as epistemically different from unwarranted error.

* Unjustified true belief. A belief can be true and still unjustified, e.g. a lucky guess. By JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not justified, so on a binary taxonomy it must also be counted as Belief. Belief is then used to cover an unwarranted state of correctness, and it is indistinguishable from a justified state of error. We lose the ability to mark lucky true belief as epistemically different from justified false belief.

Hence with only Knowledge and Belief as primitive epistemic kinds, ‘Belief’ has to simultaneously cover justified falsehood, unjustified truth and unjustified falsehood. The taxonomy is both incomplete and non-uniform: justification is invisible once truth fails, and truth is invisible once justification fails. That is why a JTB friendly taxonomy needs at least the intermediate positions JFB and UTB if we want to keep justification and truth as independently trackable epistemic values.

21.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With only Knowledge and Belief in the inventory the justification condition is essentially self-referential. If p is justified, the justification for p must be some belief q that is held about p. But q itself, if it is to do any justificatory work, must be justified. That justification must then be some belief r, and so on.

That gives you the classic regress problem: a justification for a belief requires a further justified belief to support it, which requires a further justified belief to support it, ad infinitum, with no stopping point that is actually epistemically better off than where you started.

In practice a reasoner will try to stop the chain. With knowledge and belief as the only states the only way to stop without going on forever is to stop at a belief that is not itself known. You end up having to treat some beliefs as basic, as starting points that are taken on their own authority and not themselves justified by further knowledge. That is the foundational arbitrariness/dogmatism problem: you can halt the regress only by positing a set of brute, epistemically underwritten beliefs that are simply assumed to be justified, which makes knowledge hostage to an arbitrary stopping point rather than to its own grounds. That is why JTB on this restricted resources picture is unstable.

6.text:
Under the tripartite analysis

K = J ∧ T ∧ B

the space of doxastic states is in principle 2 x 2:

Justified / Unjustified × True / False.

With only Knowledge and Belief as available categories the 2x2 is
forced into two boxes.

That forces a mis-classification.

* Justified false belief. 
JTB says a belief is knowledge iff it is justified and true. A justified
false belief is therefore not knowledge because it is false. If Belief is
the only remaining category, the justified false belief has to be
described as a mere belief. It is not a mere belief, however, because
it is justified. There is no epistemic home for a belief that is
epistemically good but false; the analysis has no state for justified
non-knowledge.

* Unjustified true belief.
JTB says a belief is knowledge iff it is justified and true. An
unjustified true belief is therefore not knowledge because it is
unjustified. If Belief is the only remaining category, the unjustified
true belief has to be described as a mere belief. It is not merely a
belief, however, because it is true. The analysis has no state for
true non-knowledge and it collapses an accidental true belief with a
genuinely epistemically deficient false belief.

Hence on a strict Knowledge / Belief taxonomy JTB cannot keep justified
belief distinct from knowledge and it cannot keep a true belief distinct
from a false belief. Justified false belief is epistemically better than
mere belief yet not knowledge, and an unjustified true belief is
factually right yet not knowledge. The two categories are therefore
over- and under-inclusive once justification and truth are treated as
independent dimensions of epistemic assessment. This is the familiar
need for an intermediate justified-belief state and for a distinct
unjustified-true-belief state, independently of the Gettier problem.

17.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With JTB and just Knowledge and Belief in the inventory you immediately run into the classic grounding problem for the Justification condition.

First, circularity. If the justification for a belief P has to be provided by a further epistemic state that is either a case of Knowledge or a mere Belief, the only way to avoid appealing to something outside the inventory is to let beliefs justify beliefs. That quickly makes any putative Knowledge P depend on some other belief Q, which in turn needs its own justification in belief R, and so on. The only way to close the chain without leaving the inventory is for the chain to loop back on itself: P is justified by Q, Q by R, ... and R by P. Knowledge is then constituted by a set of beliefs that mutually support one another, so Justification is really just internal coherence among beliefs. That is a blatant epistemic circularity, and it means Knowledge never gets an independent external anchor.

Second, the need for an arbitrary stopping point, i.e. dogmatism or foundationalism. If you try to break the circle you still have to stop the justificatory chain somewhere. You cannot stop with Knowledge, because Knowledge is itself JTB and so itself requires a prior justification. The only thing left to stop on is an unjustified Belief that you simply take as foundational. In other words, the regress is halted by stipulating a brute, ungrounded belief as a terminus for justification. That gives you a foundational base for Knowledge, but it is an arbitrary, unjustified dogma, so the Justification condition is not actually satisfied for those base beliefs and the whole JTB account inherits an ungrounded, merely stipulated starting point.

Taken together, under the restriction to Knowledge and Belief, JTB forces you either into mutually justifying belief circles or into an undefended foundational belief that is treated as known.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With the JTB analysis knowledge is a species of belief. 
K = JTB , B = ~K

If K and B are the only epistemic kinds that are available there is no independent
kind of *justification*. Justification has to be a case of K or a case of B.

* Justification as K. If to be justified in believing p is to know that p is
justified, you have to know that you know that p is justified, etc. The
justification condition is then not a condition on belief at all but a higher
order knowledge condition. That is the familiar infinite regress / circularity
of the epistemic criterion. In the limit knowledge can only be grounded in
knowledge already possessed, i.e. Meno's paradox.

* Justification as B. If to be justified in believing p is just to believe
that you are justified in believing p, or more generally to believe the
propositional grounds for p, justification adds nothing over and above belief.
A belief can then justify itself and knowledge collapses into true belief
plus a further, possibly false, belief that it is justified. Bootstrapping
and circular justification become unavoidable.

In either way the heterogeneous category B that the analysis is forced to
leave us with is the real loss. On a JTB reading

* Justified false belief is not K because it is false, and it is not
distinguishable from unjustified false belief. Both are just B
* Unjustified true belief is not K because it is unjustified, and it is not
distinguishable from false belief. Both are just B

So the epistemically very different states of a justified but false belief and
of a lucky, unjustified true belief are both lumped together under the single
label ‘belief’, and belief becomes a grab-bag of the epistemically good,
the epistemically bad and the merely accidental. That is the price of having
only the two epistemic kinds Knowledge and Belief while trying to make
knowledge Justified True Belief.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With JTB knowledge = T & B & J. If the only
epistemic labels you admit are Knowledge and Belief then everything
that is not T&B&J has to be put under Belief.

That makes Belief a heterogeneous catch-all and leaves two obvious
gaps between the two boxes.

* Justified false belief, J & B & ~T. It is justified so it is
epistemically better than a plain, or unjustified, false belief, but
because it is false it is not JTB and so on the binary taxonomy it has
to be called mere Belief. Justification is thereby lost in the Belief
box.

* Unjustified true belief, T & B & ~J. It is true so it is
epistemically better than a plain false belief, but because it is
unjustified it is not JTB and so on the binary taxonomy it has to be
called mere Belief. Truth is thereby lost in the Belief box.

In effect Belief has to do the work of three different states:
unjustified false belief, justified false belief and unjustified true
belief, while Knowledge is a proper species of Belief since K entails
B. You lose any distinct category for a rationally held false belief
and for a lucky true belief, and Belief becomes the disjunction of
justified/unjustified and true/false. That is the coarse graining
that is normally expressed as justification does not guarantee truth
and truth does not guarantee justification.

19.text:
Under JTB the epistemic space is True/False × Justified/Unjustified × Belief.

Knowledge is the one cell

K = B ∧ T ∧ J

and with only the two labels K and B available everything that is not K has to be called B.  Hence

B = ¬K = [J ∧ ¬T ∧ B] ∨ [¬J ∧ T ∧ B] ∨ [¬J ∧ ¬T ∧ B]

i.e. Belief is the disjunctive residual of the three remaining cells. In particular

* Justified false belief J ∧ ¬T. It is not knowledge because it fails truth, so on the two state taxonomy it must be called mere belief. Belief is therefore forced to contain justified states, and justified false belief is indistinguishable from unjustified false belief.

* Unjustified true belief ¬J ∧ T. It is not knowledge because it fails justification, so on the two state taxonomy it must be called mere belief. Belief is therefore forced to contain true states, and an unjustified lucky true belief is indistinguishable from a false belief.

So K is a proper species of B, K→B, the categories are not exclusive, and Belief becomes a heterogeneous catch-all that is simultaneously justified and unjustified, true and false.  The normative difference between a justified false belief and an unjustified false belief, and the truth difference between an unjustified true belief and a false belief, are lost on the Knowledge/Belief dichotomy. That is the price of having no intermediate epistemic categories such as justified belief, true belief, justified false belief etc.

11.text:
With JTB Knowledge = JTB and the only other state is Belief the residual
category Belief has to do the work of three different epistemic profiles.

* JTB  = Knowledge
* J ~T  = justified false belief
* T ~J  = unjustified true belief
* ~J ~T = unjustified false belief

If Knowledge is JTB there is no place to put a belief which is justified
but false and no place to put a belief which is true but unjustified. Both
have to be called mere Belief.

That gives two, and with ~J~T three, distinct problems that are all
conflated under one label:

1. Justified false belief.  A belief can be properly justified and yet
false – e.g. a well supported scientific conjecture that turns out to be
false.  On JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not true.  If Belief is
the only non-Knowledge state the justified false belief is lumped together
with unjustified false belief and with unjustified true belief.  Justification
is therefore lost as an independent mark of epistemic value: a justified
false belief is treated as just a belief on a par with an unjustified false
belief.

2. Unjustified true belief.  A belief can be true and believed but
unjustified – e.g. a lucky guess, a hunch that happens to be right.  On JTB
it is not Knowledge because it is not justified.  With only Knowledge and
Belief as options it is also just Belief, so it is lumped together with a
justified false belief and with an unjustified false belief.  Truth is
therefore lost as an independent mark of epistemic value: an unjustified
true belief is treated as just a belief on a par with a justified false
belief.

Hence belief becomes a heterogeneous umbrella for J~T, T~J and ~J~T.  In
particular the intuitively distinct cases of a justified false belief and
an unjustified true belief cannot be distinguished from one another, or
from plainly bad unjustified false belief, once the only recognised
non-knowledge state is Belief.  That is the loss of the independent
epistemic roles of justification and of truth.

15.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With knowledge = justified true belief there are four
truth x justification combinations that the tripartite analysis has to
locate,

T J,  T ~J,  ~T J,  ~T ~J

If the only locative categories you have are Knowledge and mere Belief
then T J has to be Knowledge and everything else is just Belief. That
forces an unwanted collapse.

* Justified false belief.  ~T J is epistemically good in the sense that
the belief is properly supported, but it is not Knowledge because it is
not true. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it is just a Belief and
so it is indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief ~T ~J. You
lose the ability to mark a justified false belief as a respectably
justified, albeit false, epistemic state.

* Unjustified true belief.  T ~J is true in the world but it is not
Knowledge because it lacks justification. On a Knowledge/Belief only
taxonomy it is just a Belief and so it is indistinguishable from a
justified false belief ~T J. You lose the ability to mark a true belief
by luck/accident as epistemically deficient. Unjustified true belief
and justified false belief become the same unmarked class, mere
Belief.

Hence JTB with only Knowledge and Belief at its disposal can mark
justified true belief as knowledge, but it cannot keep apart justified
false belief from unjustified false belief and it cannot keep apart
unjustified true belief from justified false belief. The justification
condition comes apart from the truth condition, and the two
intuitively distinct non-knowledge states are forced into the single
residual category of Belief. That is the familiar justification-truth
gap that underlies the later need for a richer taxonomy of justified
belief and of true belief.

18.text:
**PUBLIC RESPONSE:** With JTB there are formally three ingredients, B,T and J. If the taxonomy is closed to Knowledge and bare Belief, J can only ever show up as part of Knowledge, K = JTB. Belief then becomes the residual category for everything which is not JTB.

That residue is heterogeneous and J is lost as an independent epistemic mark.

1. Justified false belief. Intuitively a well-supported false belief is epistemically good even though it is not knowledge. Under the Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must be classified as mere Belief, and it is thereby lumped with arbitrary, groundless false beliefs. Justification ceases to be recognisable as a good when truth fails, because there is no state ‘justified belief’ in which to house it. That is the familiar justification without truth problem.

2. True belief without justification. Intuitively a true belief that is held by luck is epistemically defective even though it is true. Under the Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must again be classified as mere Belief, and it is thereby lumped with justified false beliefs. The distinction between warranted truth and lucky truth is lost, because there is no state ‘unjustified but true belief’ in which to house the defect. That is the familiar true-but-lucky belief problem.

Hence Belief becomes a grab-bag of justified false beliefs, unjustified true beliefs and completely groundless beliefs. In the usual way of putting it justification cannot be an autonomous epistemic state: if justification is itself to be known it generates the regress / circularity problem,  know p requires know that you are justified in believing p requires know that you are justified in believing that you are justified… etc. If justification is itself a belief it is not truth-conducive. That is why the taxonomy is normally expanded beyond Knowledge and Belief to a genuine justified belief state.

20.text:
With JTB

K(p)  <->  B(p) & J(p) & T(p)

the only thing you can ever attribute to an agent is K or B.  K already contains
B,J,T.  So once you have thrown away the independent attitude of
justified-belief the justificatory and the truth dimensions can only be read
off the K/B boundary.  The state space becomes too coarse to track
justification independently of truth.

That coarse-graining gives you two non-Gettier losses of discriminatory power.

* Loss of epistemic credit for good reasons that happen to be false.
  A justified false belief satisfies J(p) & B(p) & ~T(p).  On JTB it is not
  knowledge, so the only attribution you can make is B(p). That is the same
  attribution you would make for an unjustified false belief.  Justification
  is therefore invisible once truth fails: you have no epistemic state in
  which an agent can be in a good epistemic position with respect to p while
  p is false.  In effect justification is only ever a live dimension when
  T(p) is already secured.

* Loss of epistemic demerit for true belief by luck.
  An unjustified true belief satisfies B(p) & T(p) & ~J(p).  On JTB it is
  not knowledge, so the only attribution you can make is B(p) again.  Now
  B(p) is the same attribution you would make for a justified false belief
  and for an unjustified false belief.  Truth is therefore invisible once
  justification fails: you have no epistemic state in which you can mark a
  true belief as epistemically defective, i.e. as mere luck, as opposed to a
  justified true belief which you are forced to count as knowledge.

In ordinary talk this is the familiar over- and under-generation of
knowledge.  You cannot mark a justified false belief as epistemically better
than an unjustified false belief, and you cannot mark an unjustified true
belief as epistemically worse than a justified true belief.  With only K and
B available every justified true belief is forced up to knowledge – the
lottery/preface type over-intellectualisation – and every justified false
belief or lucky true belief is forced down to bare belief, so the
justificatory value of a false belief and the un-warrantedness of a true
belief are both erased.  That is the coarse-graining that makes JTB
uninformative once the independent category of justified belief is removed.

public_text.1:
On a JTB analysis knowledge is not a primitive, it is a complex
of belief + truth + justification. With only Knowledge and Belief as
primitive epistemic locutions the truth / justification square cannot be
kept straight.

Truth x Justification gives in the ordinary taxonomy four places

* JTB = Knowledge
* JT¬B? i.e. justified true belief = Knowledge by JTB
* J¬TB = justified false belief
* ¬JTB = unjustified true belief
* ¬J¬TB = unjustified false belief

Knowledge is taken to entail belief, so the only thing a JTB
analysis can mark off from mere belief is the JTB cell. Every
proposition that is not known therefore has to be filed under the
single label ‘belief’. That is

1. an inability to keep justified false belief distinct from an
unjustified false belief, and more generally to keep justified belief
distinct from unjustified belief.  A justified false belief is, on JTB,
epistemically good but not knowledge because it is not true.  With
only the two primitives Knowledge / Belief the justification component
has to be expressed in terms of Knowledge or in terms of Belief. If it
is expressed in terms of Belief you get a regress of beliefs for
justification: p is justified by belief q, q by belief r, … ad
infinitum, so justification never terminates in a distinct epistemic
state.  If it is expressed in terms of Knowledge you have circularity:
p is justified because it is known, but p is known only if it is
justified.  In ordinary language the loss appears as the collapse of
justified false belief into mere belief, i.e. the loss of an
epistemically creditworthy non-knowledge state.

2. an inability to keep unjustified true belief distinct from a
justified true belief.  An unjustified true belief is true but not
knowledge.  On the JTB taxonomy it is forced into the single ‘belief’
bin together with justified false belief and unjustified false belief.
Hence you lose the distinction between a true belief that is lucky and
a true belief that is creditable, and justification becomes idle once
truth is secured.  That is the familiar regress / circularity
formulation in the other direction: if justification is tried to be
made out of further beliefs you have the infinite regress of
justification; if you try to stop the regress with knowledge you have
justification = knowledge and JTB is circular.

In practice the two cells that JTB needs but that a two-state
ontology cannot accommodate are the creditworthy but non-knowledge
justified false belief and the lucky but non-knowledge unjustified true
belief.  That is the 2×2 truth/justification collapse that is normally
displayed as the regress of beliefs-for-justification versus the
circularity of knowledge-for-justification.
public_text.2:
The JTB picture with only Knowledge and Belief as resources for justification runs straight into the classic regress/terminus dilemma.

If a belief p is justified, its justification must itself be a justified belief q, and q in turn must be justified by a justified belief r, and so on. With only Belief and Knowledge available as the kinds of epistemic attitudes that can do justifying work, you cannot appeal to a non-doxastic warrant, so the chain of beliefs that is supposed to justify p has to be built out of further beliefs. That gives you an infinite regress of ever further justifying beliefs with no stopping point.

The alternative to letting the regress run forever is to stop the chain at some point and say that certain beliefs are justified simply in virtue of being held, i.e., to posit a class of basic or foundational beliefs that are taken as epistemically given. On a strictly belief/knowledge-only inventory that stopping point is just dogmatism: you end up with beliefs that are treated as justified even though they themselves enjoy no independent justification within the system, an arbitrary foundation for the rest of the justificatory structure. Those two pressures — endless justification or an arbitrary, ungrounded foundation — are the structural problems JTB faces once you restrict the epistemic menu to Knowledge and Belief alone.
public_text.5: With only knowledge and belief in the toolbox, justification for a belief can only be supplied by another belief or by an item you already count as knowledge. That immediately generates the familiar regress worry: any belief you offer as a reason for p has to itself be justified, which demands a further belief/reason, and so on ad infinitum, with no non-question-begging way to halt the chain. The only way to stop the chain in principle is to posit some beliefs that are taken to be justified without themselves being justified by any further knowledge or belief — an arbitrary foundational stop or epistemic dogmatism. In other words JTB is forced either into an endless demand for further reasons or into resting the whole edifice on an unjustified, stipulated base, and neither option gives a satisfying account of justification on a purely belief/knowledge ontology.
public_text.7: With only Knowledge and Belief as live epistemic options, the justification clause in JTB forces a justificatory chain that can’t be closed. First you get the familiar infinite regress: to justify belief B you need a further belief B1 that B is justified, to justify B1 you need B2, and so on, because any justifier you can appeal to will itself be a belief that then needs justification. If you try to avoid the regress you are left with having to stop the chain at some point. But the only states you have are Knowledge, which by definition already requires justification, and Belief, which by itself is not knowledge. So the stopping point can only be an unjustified but taken-for-granted belief. That is the problem of an arbitrary or dogmatic foundation: you have to posit a baseline belief that is simply accepted without justification, which makes the account of knowledge rest on an epistemically unmotivated fiat rather than on genuine justification.
public_text.14:
With only Knowledge and Belief as our epistemic resources, justification for a belief can only be supplied by something we already know or by something we merely believe. That generates two standard pressures.

First, the regress problem. If a belief p is justified only insofar as it is supported by a further belief q, and q itself needs justification, then justification can only be secured by a still further belief r, and so on. On a demanding reading where the justifier itself must be known, you never actually get off the ground without an infinite chain of justifiers.

Second, if the chain cannot be infinite, you have to stop it somewhere. Stopping it means positing some beliefs that are taken to be justified without themselves being justified by further knowledge or belief. Those would be epistemically arbitrary or dogmatic foundational beliefs. In effect you are forced to accept a base of beliefs whose justification is simply assumed, which is the classic problem of an unjustified stopping point / foundational dogmatism.

So the JTB picture with only knowledge and belief available is squeezed between an unending regress of justifiers and having to arbitrarily halt the regress with basic beliefs that are not themselves justified.
public_text.13:
If justification is itself an epistemic state then with only knowledge and belief to work with every justification for a belief P has to be either a piece of knowledge or a further belief about P. 

That immediately gives the classic regress of justification: a belief is justified only if the beliefs that justify it are themselves justified, and those justifiers need justifiers, etc. There is no third epistemic state to stop the chain, so in principle you are driven to an infinite hierarchy of ever higher-order justifications.

Because the regress cannot be run forever in practice, the only way to halt it is to posit some beliefs that are taken as basic or self-warranting and are simply left unjustified. With the inventory restricted to knowledge and belief that stopping point is just an arbitrary foundational dogmatism: basic beliefs are accepted as the terminus of justification even though they are not themselves known or justified in the JTB sense, so knowledge collapses into well-founded but ultimately groundless belief. The justificatory role is then played by belief all the way down, which blurs the intended distinction between justified true belief as knowledge and mere true belief.
public_text.16:
With only Knowledge and Belief in the inventory the justification condition for JTB becomes self-consuming. 

First, any justified belief P must be justified by some further belief or beliefs Q1...Qn that the subject holds. If those Qs are only beliefs, they too must be justified in order for them to count as justifiers for P under JTB. That pushes the demand for a justifier one step back again, and so on. On the assumption that no belief can count as a justifier unless it is itself justified, you get an infinite regress of justifiers for justifiers.

Second, the regress can only be stopped, if it is to be stopped within the Knowledge/Belief inventory, by terminating the chain in beliefs that are not themselves justified. That is, you end up having to treat some set of basic beliefs as justified simply by being believed, or as justified simply in virtue of being known. The first option is an arbitrary, dogmatic foundation, the second collapses justification into knowledge. In either case you are forced to accept a class of epistemic states that are held to be justified without any further epistemic support, i.e. an ungrounded, dogmatic base for the whole JTB structure. That is the classic foundational/arbitrariness problem that appears alongside the regress when no third epistemic status between knowledge and mere belief is available.
public_text.9:
With JTB the justification condition has to be cashable in the epistemic resources you already have. If the only resources are Knowledge and Belief, then the reason you give for P must itself be a belief Q. Q is itself a belief, so on the JTB picture it too needs justification, and whatever justifies Q is a further belief R, and so on. That is the classic infinite regress of ever higher-order beliefs about beliefs.

The regress can only be stopped by allowing a chain to bottom out. But bottoming out on the resources here means either bottoming out in a belief that is treated as a terminus of justification even though it is not itself justified, i.e. a dogmatic or arbitrary stopping point, or bottoming out in a knowledge claim that already presupposes the very justification you are trying to secure. In either case you end up with an epistemic gap: you need a foundational class of beliefs that are taken to be justified in virtue of being held, or you need to posit a primitive knowledge base that is not itself produced by JTB, so the account can no longer explain how a mere belief is transformed into knowledge without smuggling in an extra epistemic status. That is why JTB on a two-state inventory faces the regress problem together with the problem of having to appeal to unjustified, essentially dogmatic foundations to block the regress.
public_text.4:
With JTB knowledge = justified true belief the epistemic taxonomy is exhausted by

* K = justified & true & believed
* B = not-K

so every non-knowledge state is just *belief*. Belief therefore has to do the work of four distinct intuitive states: justified true, unjustified true, justified false and unjustified false. The category B is then massively heterogeneous.

That gives you two independent collapses.

1. **Justified false belief is conflated with unjustified false belief.**  
A JFB is epistemically valuable in the way an unjustified false belief is not, but on JTB with only K and B it is not knowledge because it is false and it is not a distinct epistemic kind, it is just belief. Justification therefore ceases to matter for the class of false beliefs: justified false belief and unjustified false belief are both simply ‘belief’.

2. **Unjustified true belief is conflated with false belief.**  
An UTB is true in a way a false belief is not, but on JTB with only K and B it is not knowledge because it is unjustified and it is not a distinct epistemic kind, it is just belief. Truth therefore ceases to matter for the class of non-justified beliefs: an unjustified true belief and an unjustified false belief, and indeed a justified false belief, are all simply ‘belief’.

Hence Belief ends up lumping together justified with unjustified and true with false. JTB cannot capture the independent epistemic value of justification apart from truth and the independent epistemic value of truth apart from justification. That is the classic need for intermediate states such as justified belief, true belief, justified false belief, etc., which the two-state K / B taxonomy cannot accommodate.
public_text.3:
Under JTB

K p  iff  B p & T p & J p

and with only the two labels K and B to work with the four J x T cells
are forced into two bins

J T : JTB = Knowledge
J ~T : justified false belief
~J T : unjustified true belief
~J ~T : unjustified false belief

are all mapped onto B except the first one. That coarse graining is
the trouble.

* Justification does not entail truth. A subject can be fully justified
in holding p and still be wrong. JFB is on the same epistemic
label as an unjustified false belief, mere Belief. With only K and B
at our disposal we have no way to mark the epistemically responsible
false belief off from an irresponsible false belief, justification is
lost as soon as the belief turns out false.

* Truth does not entail justification. A subject can believe p truly
by luck, coincidence, wishful thinking etc., and p will still be
only a Belief. JTB therefore makes an unjustified true belief
epistemically indistinguishable from a justified false belief: both are
just Belief. In particular the epistemic value of justification for a
true belief is invisible until the belief is made true, and the
epistemic responsibility carried by a justified false belief is
invisible once the belief is false. That is the familiar justified-false
belief / accidental-true-belief gap which forces the whole J × T
space into the Knowledge / Belief dichotomy.
public_text.8:
On a JTB analysis Knowledge = True + Justified + Belief. If the ontology of doxastic states is really exhausted by Knowledge and Belief, then Belief is the residual class of everything that is not Knowledge.

That residual class is heterogeneous.

* Justified false belief. A belief can be justified and still false. By JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not true, so on a binary taxonomy it must be counted as Belief. Belief is then used to cover a justified state of error, and it is indistinguishable from an unjustified state of error. We lose the ability to mark warranted error as epistemically different from unwarranted error.

* Unjustified true belief. A belief can be true and still unjustified, e.g. a lucky guess. By JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not justified, so on a binary taxonomy it must also be counted as Belief. Belief is then used to cover an unwarranted state of correctness, and it is indistinguishable from a justified state of error. We lose the ability to mark lucky true belief as epistemically different from justified false belief.

Hence with only Knowledge and Belief as primitive epistemic kinds, ‘Belief’ has to simultaneously cover justified falsehood, unjustified truth and unjustified falsehood. The taxonomy is both incomplete and non-uniform: justification is invisible once truth fails, and truth is invisible once justification fails. That is why a JTB friendly taxonomy needs at least the intermediate positions JFB and UTB if we want to keep justification and truth as independently trackable epistemic values.
public_text.21:
With only Knowledge and Belief in the inventory the justification condition is essentially self-referential. If p is justified, the justification for p must be some belief q that is held about p. But q itself, if it is to do any justificatory work, must be justified. That justification must then be some belief r, and so on.

That gives you the classic regress problem: a justification for a belief requires a further justified belief to support it, which requires a further justified belief to support it, ad infinitum, with no stopping point that is actually epistemically better off than where you started.

In practice a reasoner will try to stop the chain. With knowledge and belief as the only states the only way to stop without going on forever is to stop at a belief that is not itself known. You end up having to treat some beliefs as basic, as starting points that are taken on their own authority and not themselves justified by further knowledge. That is the foundational arbitrariness/dogmatism problem: you can halt the regress only by positing a set of brute, epistemically underwritten beliefs that are simply assumed to be justified, which makes knowledge hostage to an arbitrary stopping point rather than to its own grounds. That is why JTB on this restricted resources picture is unstable.
public_text.6:
Under the tripartite analysis

K = J ∧ T ∧ B

the space of doxastic states is in principle 2 x 2:

Justified / Unjustified × True / False.

With only Knowledge and Belief as available categories the 2x2 is
forced into two boxes.

That forces a mis-classification.

* Justified false belief. 
JTB says a belief is knowledge iff it is justified and true. A justified
false belief is therefore not knowledge because it is false. If Belief is
the only remaining category, the justified false belief has to be
described as a mere belief. It is not a mere belief, however, because
it is justified. There is no epistemic home for a belief that is
epistemically good but false; the analysis has no state for justified
non-knowledge.

* Unjustified true belief.
JTB says a belief is knowledge iff it is justified and true. An
unjustified true belief is therefore not knowledge because it is
unjustified. If Belief is the only remaining category, the unjustified
true belief has to be described as a mere belief. It is not merely a
belief, however, because it is true. The analysis has no state for
true non-knowledge and it collapses an accidental true belief with a
genuinely epistemically deficient false belief.

Hence on a strict Knowledge / Belief taxonomy JTB cannot keep justified
belief distinct from knowledge and it cannot keep a true belief distinct
from a false belief. Justified false belief is epistemically better than
mere belief yet not knowledge, and an unjustified true belief is
factually right yet not knowledge. The two categories are therefore
over- and under-inclusive once justification and truth are treated as
independent dimensions of epistemic assessment. This is the familiar
need for an intermediate justified-belief state and for a distinct
unjustified-true-belief state, independently of the Gettier problem.
public_text.17:
With JTB and just Knowledge and Belief in the inventory you immediately run into the classic grounding problem for the Justification condition.

First, circularity. If the justification for a belief P has to be provided by a further epistemic state that is either a case of Knowledge or a mere Belief, the only way to avoid appealing to something outside the inventory is to let beliefs justify beliefs. That quickly makes any putative Knowledge P depend on some other belief Q, which in turn needs its own justification in belief R, and so on. The only way to close the chain without leaving the inventory is for the chain to loop back on itself: P is justified by Q, Q by R, ... and R by P. Knowledge is then constituted by a set of beliefs that mutually support one another, so Justification is really just internal coherence among beliefs. That is a blatant epistemic circularity, and it means Knowledge never gets an independent external anchor.

Second, the need for an arbitrary stopping point, i.e. dogmatism or foundationalism. If you try to break the circle you still have to stop the justificatory chain somewhere. You cannot stop with Knowledge, because Knowledge is itself JTB and so itself requires a prior justification. The only thing left to stop on is an unjustified Belief that you simply take as foundational. In other words, the regress is halted by stipulating a brute, ungrounded belief as a terminus for justification. That gives you a foundational base for Knowledge, but it is an arbitrary, unjustified dogma, so the Justification condition is not actually satisfied for those base beliefs and the whole JTB account inherits an ungrounded, merely stipulated starting point.

Taken together, under the restriction to Knowledge and Belief, JTB forces you either into mutually justifying belief circles or into an undefended foundational belief that is treated as known.
public_text.10:
With the JTB analysis knowledge is a species of belief. 
K = JTB , B = ~K

If K and B are the only epistemic kinds that are available there is no independent
kind of *justification*. Justification has to be a case of K or a case of B.

* Justification as K. If to be justified in believing p is to know that p is
justified, you have to know that you know that p is justified, etc. The
justification condition is then not a condition on belief at all but a higher
order knowledge condition. That is the familiar infinite regress / circularity
of the epistemic criterion. In the limit knowledge can only be grounded in
knowledge already possessed, i.e. Meno's paradox.

* Justification as B. If to be justified in believing p is just to believe
that you are justified in believing p, or more generally to believe the
propositional grounds for p, justification adds nothing over and above belief.
A belief can then justify itself and knowledge collapses into true belief
plus a further, possibly false, belief that it is justified. Bootstrapping
and circular justification become unavoidable.

In either way the heterogeneous category B that the analysis is forced to
leave us with is the real loss. On a JTB reading

* Justified false belief is not K because it is false, and it is not
distinguishable from unjustified false belief. Both are just B
* Unjustified true belief is not K because it is unjustified, and it is not
distinguishable from false belief. Both are just B

So the epistemically very different states of a justified but false belief and
of a lucky, unjustified true belief are both lumped together under the single
label ‘belief’, and belief becomes a grab-bag of the epistemically good,
the epistemically bad and the merely accidental. That is the price of having
only the two epistemic kinds Knowledge and Belief while trying to make
knowledge Justified True Belief.
public_text.12:
With JTB knowledge = T & B & J. If the only
epistemic labels you admit are Knowledge and Belief then everything
that is not T&B&J has to be put under Belief.

That makes Belief a heterogeneous catch-all and leaves two obvious
gaps between the two boxes.

* Justified false belief, J & B & ~T. It is justified so it is
epistemically better than a plain, or unjustified, false belief, but
because it is false it is not JTB and so on the binary taxonomy it has
to be called mere Belief. Justification is thereby lost in the Belief
box.

* Unjustified true belief, T & B & ~J. It is true so it is
epistemically better than a plain false belief, but because it is
unjustified it is not JTB and so on the binary taxonomy it has to be
called mere Belief. Truth is thereby lost in the Belief box.

In effect Belief has to do the work of three different states:
unjustified false belief, justified false belief and unjustified true
belief, while Knowledge is a proper species of Belief since K entails
B. You lose any distinct category for a rationally held false belief
and for a lucky true belief, and Belief becomes the disjunction of
justified/unjustified and true/false. That is the coarse graining
that is normally expressed as justification does not guarantee truth
and truth does not guarantee justification.
public_text.19:
Under JTB the epistemic space is True/False × Justified/Unjustified × Belief.

Knowledge is the one cell

K = B ∧ T ∧ J

and with only the two labels K and B available everything that is not K has to be called B.  Hence

B = ¬K = [J ∧ ¬T ∧ B] ∨ [¬J ∧ T ∧ B] ∨ [¬J ∧ ¬T ∧ B]

i.e. Belief is the disjunctive residual of the three remaining cells. In particular

* Justified false belief J ∧ ¬T. It is not knowledge because it fails truth, so on the two state taxonomy it must be called mere belief. Belief is therefore forced to contain justified states, and justified false belief is indistinguishable from unjustified false belief.

* Unjustified true belief ¬J ∧ T. It is not knowledge because it fails justification, so on the two state taxonomy it must be called mere belief. Belief is therefore forced to contain true states, and an unjustified lucky true belief is indistinguishable from a false belief.

So K is a proper species of B, K→B, the categories are not exclusive, and Belief becomes a heterogeneous catch-all that is simultaneously justified and unjustified, true and false.  The normative difference between a justified false belief and an unjustified false belief, and the truth difference between an unjustified true belief and a false belief, are lost on the Knowledge/Belief dichotomy. That is the price of having no intermediate epistemic categories such as justified belief, true belief, justified false belief etc.
public_text.11:
With JTB Knowledge = JTB and the only other state is Belief the residual
category Belief has to do the work of three different epistemic profiles.

* JTB  = Knowledge
* J ~T  = justified false belief
* T ~J  = unjustified true belief
* ~J ~T = unjustified false belief

If Knowledge is JTB there is no place to put a belief which is justified
but false and no place to put a belief which is true but unjustified. Both
have to be called mere Belief.

That gives two, and with ~J~T three, distinct problems that are all
conflated under one label:

1. Justified false belief.  A belief can be properly justified and yet
false – e.g. a well supported scientific conjecture that turns out to be
false.  On JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not true.  If Belief is
the only non-Knowledge state the justified false belief is lumped together
with unjustified false belief and with unjustified true belief.  Justification
is therefore lost as an independent mark of epistemic value: a justified
false belief is treated as just a belief on a par with an unjustified false
belief.

2. Unjustified true belief.  A belief can be true and believed but
unjustified – e.g. a lucky guess, a hunch that happens to be right.  On JTB
it is not Knowledge because it is not justified.  With only Knowledge and
Belief as options it is also just Belief, so it is lumped together with a
justified false belief and with an unjustified false belief.  Truth is
therefore lost as an independent mark of epistemic value: an unjustified
true belief is treated as just a belief on a par with a justified false
belief.

Hence belief becomes a heterogeneous umbrella for J~T, T~J and ~J~T.  In
particular the intuitively distinct cases of a justified false belief and
an unjustified true belief cannot be distinguished from one another, or
from plainly bad unjustified false belief, once the only recognised
non-knowledge state is Belief.  That is the loss of the independent
epistemic roles of justification and of truth.
public_text.15:
With knowledge = justified true belief there are four
truth x justification combinations that the tripartite analysis has to
locate,

T J,  T ~J,  ~T J,  ~T ~J

If the only locative categories you have are Knowledge and mere Belief
then T J has to be Knowledge and everything else is just Belief. That
forces an unwanted collapse.

* Justified false belief.  ~T J is epistemically good in the sense that
the belief is properly supported, but it is not Knowledge because it is
not true. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it is just a Belief and
so it is indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief ~T ~J. You
lose the ability to mark a justified false belief as a respectably
justified, albeit false, epistemic state.

* Unjustified true belief.  T ~J is true in the world but it is not
Knowledge because it lacks justification. On a Knowledge/Belief only
taxonomy it is just a Belief and so it is indistinguishable from a
justified false belief ~T J. You lose the ability to mark a true belief
by luck/accident as epistemically deficient. Unjustified true belief
and justified false belief become the same unmarked class, mere
Belief.

Hence JTB with only Knowledge and Belief at its disposal can mark
justified true belief as knowledge, but it cannot keep apart justified
false belief from unjustified false belief and it cannot keep apart
unjustified true belief from justified false belief. The justification
condition comes apart from the truth condition, and the two
intuitively distinct non-knowledge states are forced into the single
residual category of Belief. That is the familiar justification-truth
gap that underlies the later need for a richer taxonomy of justified
belief and of true belief.
public_text.18:
With JTB there are formally three ingredients, B,T and J. If the taxonomy is closed to Knowledge and bare Belief, J can only ever show up as part of Knowledge, K = JTB. Belief then becomes the residual category for everything which is not JTB.

That residue is heterogeneous and J is lost as an independent epistemic mark.

1. Justified false belief. Intuitively a well-supported false belief is epistemically good even though it is not knowledge. Under the Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must be classified as mere Belief, and it is thereby lumped with arbitrary, groundless false beliefs. Justification ceases to be recognisable as a good when truth fails, because there is no state ‘justified belief’ in which to house it. That is the familiar justification without truth problem.

2. True belief without justification. Intuitively a true belief that is held by luck is epistemically defective even though it is true. Under the Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must again be classified as mere Belief, and it is thereby lumped with justified false beliefs. The distinction between warranted truth and lucky truth is lost, because there is no state ‘unjustified but true belief’ in which to house the defect. That is the familiar true-but-lucky belief problem.

Hence Belief becomes a grab-bag of justified false beliefs, unjustified true beliefs and completely groundless beliefs. In the usual way of putting it justification cannot be an autonomous epistemic state: if justification is itself to be known it generates the regress / circularity problem,  know p requires know that you are justified in believing p requires know that you are justified in believing that you are justified… etc. If justification is itself a belief it is not truth-conducive. That is why the taxonomy is normally expanded beyond Knowledge and Belief to a genuine justified belief state.
public_text.20:
With JTB

K(p)  <->  B(p) & J(p) & T(p)

the only thing you can ever attribute to an agent is K or B.  K already contains
B,J,T.  So once you have thrown away the independent attitude of
justified-belief the justificatory and the truth dimensions can only be read
off the K/B boundary.  The state space becomes too coarse to track
justification independently of truth.

That coarse-graining gives you two non-Gettier losses of discriminatory power.

* Loss of epistemic credit for good reasons that happen to be false.
  A justified false belief satisfies J(p) & B(p) & ~T(p).  On JTB it is not
  knowledge, so the only attribution you can make is B(p). That is the same
  attribution you would make for an unjustified false belief.  Justification
  is therefore invisible once truth fails: you have no epistemic state in
  which an agent can be in a good epistemic position with respect to p while
  p is false.  In effect justification is only ever a live dimension when
  T(p) is already secured.

* Loss of epistemic demerit for true belief by luck.
  An unjustified true belief satisfies B(p) & T(p) & ~J(p).  On JTB it is
  not knowledge, so the only attribution you can make is B(p) again.  Now
  B(p) is the same attribution you would make for a justified false belief
  and for an unjustified false belief.  Truth is therefore invisible once
  justification fails: you have no epistemic state in which you can mark a
  true belief as epistemically defective, i.e. as mere luck, as opposed to a
  justified true belief which you are forced to count as knowledge.

In ordinary talk this is the familiar over- and under-generation of
knowledge.  You cannot mark a justified false belief as epistemically better
than an unjustified false belief, and you cannot mark an unjustified true
belief as epistemically worse than a justified true belief.  With only K and
B available every justified true belief is forced up to knowledge – the
lottery/preface type over-intellectualisation – and every justified false
belief or lucky true belief is forced down to bare belief, so the
justificatory value of a false belief and the un-warrantedness of a true
belief are both erased.  That is the coarse-graining that makes JTB
uninformative once the independent category of justified belief is removed.

That makes Belief heterogeneous. The 2×2 truth × justification space collapses:
* JT = K

* ¬JT = unjustified true belief

T J = K
~T J = justified false belief
T ~J = unjustified true belief
~T ~J = unjustified false belief

If everything non-K must be called Belief, Belief becomes the disjunction [J∧~T∧B] ∨ [~J∧T∧B] ∨ [~J∧~T∧B]. K is a proper species of B, K→B, and the residual category is heterogeneous.

That yields the taxonomic loss everybody flags:
* Justified false belief, J∧B∧~T. It is not K because it is false, so the two-state taxonomy forces it into mere Belief. Justification is therefore invisible once truth fails; justified false belief is indistinguishable from unjustified false belief.
* Unjustified true belief, T∧B∧~J. It is not K because it is unjustified, so it too is forced into mere Belief. Truth is therefore invisible once justification fails; an accidental/lucky true belief is indistinguishable from a justified false belief and from plain unjustified false belief.

Hence Belief has to do the work of three different profiles – justified false, unjustified true, unjustified false – and the independent normative marks of justification and truth are lost on the K/B dichotomy.

Several colleagues restate the same loss as a grounding problem for the justification condition. With no independent justified-belief state, justification for p can only be supplied by a further belief q or by a piece of knowledge. If justified by belief, justification must be justified in turn, giving an infinite regress of ever higher-order justifiers; if justification is identified with knowledge, justification = knowledge and JTB is circular. Halting the chain requires a set of basic beliefs that are taken as justified without further justification – an arbitrary foundational dogmatism.

So the discussion presents two intertwined pressures: the collapse of J~T and T~J into the undifferentiated Belief bin, and the consequent regress/circularity versus dogmatic foundation dilemma for cashing out justification in the K/B inventory alone. The Gettier problem is explicitly set aside. Unresolved in the current material is whether the primary statement of the problem should be given as the taxonomic conflation of justified false vs unjustified false and unjustified true vs justified false, or as the more familiar regress/foundation formulation; most contributors treat them as two sides of the same coarse-graining.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The JTB analysis needs three independent dimensions B, T, J. K = B∧T∧J. With only the two locutions Knowledge and Belief available, everything that is not K is forced into the residual category Belief.

That forces a 2×2 Truth×Justification space into two boxes:
* JT = Knowledge
* J~T = justified false belief
* ~JT = unjustified true belief
* ~J~T = unjustified false belief

are all mapped onto ‘mere Belief’ except the first. Belief is therefore a heterogeneous catch-all K→B. Knowledge is a proper species of belief.

The consensus collapse account from Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8 is:
1. Justification is lost once truth fails. A justified false belief J∧B∧~T is not K and has no home; it must be called Belief. It is therefore indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief ~J∧B∧~T and from an unjustified true belief. The epistemic credit of a properly supported but false belief is erased; justification cannot be marked as an independent value apart from truth.
2. Truth is lost once justification fails. An unjustified true belief T∧B∧~J is not K and has no home; it must be called Belief. It is therefore indistinguishable from a justified false belief J∧B∧~T and from an unjustified false belief. The epistemic defect of a lucky true belief is erased; truth cannot be marked as an independent value apart from justification. Belief becomes the disjunction of J~T, ~JT and ~J~T.

Several colleagues formalise the loss as regress/circularity/dogmatism for the Justification condition. With only K and B as epistemic resources, a justifier for p must be a belief q or a knowledge k. If it is a belief, q itself needs justification, giving an infinite regress of ever higher order beliefs. The only stops are:
* circularity / bootstrapping: justification is made out of knowledge, i.e. p is justified because it is known, which is circular, or beliefs mutually justify each other;
* arbitrary foundationalism: a base of beliefs is taken as justified simply in virtue of being believed, an ungrounded dogmatic terminus.

Colleagues 2,5,7,9,13,14,16,17,21 present that regress vs arbitrary stopping point as the two pressures generated by the two-state ontology. The regress pressure and the dogmatic foundation pressure are the justificatory expression of the coarse-graining just described: justification cannot be an autonomous epistemic mark because it can only be cashed out in K or B.

Disagreement to track: some colleagues frame the “two problems” as the two non-knowledge cells J~T and ~JT being conflated under Belief; others frame them as infinite regress vs foundational arbitrariness / circularity. Both point to the same underlying loss of an independent justified-belief state and an independent true-belief state once the inventory is restricted to Knowledge and Belief. Unresolved is whether the required answer is expressed as a taxonomic collapse or as a meta-justificatory regress/dogmatism problem; the literature treats them as two sides of the same coarse-graining.

I retain the core claim: with K/B only, JTB cannot keep justified false belief distinct from unjustified false belief and cannot keep unjustified true belief distinct from justified false belief/unjustified false belief, with the attendant regress/circularity/dogmatism consequence for trying to cash justification in terms of K/B alone. Gettier is explicitly excluded.
